## 2. Subcritical case: proof of Theorem 1.3

### 2.1. Surjectivity of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$

Assume in this section that $\delta$ is large. Then we wish to show that $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ is surjective. We follow the plan outlined in Section 1.5.1. By translating $A,B$ , assume without loss of generality that all points in $A,B$ have magnitude $\gtrsim\delta^{\varpi}$ , where $\varpi\gtrsim 1$ is fixed. In particular, since $\delta$ is large, all points have magnitude $\geq 1$ .

For $a_{0}\in A$ , let $\varphi_{a_{0}}$ be a bump function adapted to

$$ \displaystyle\{|x-a_{0}|\lesssim|a_{0}|^{-p}\}, $$

with $\varphi_{a_{0}}(a_{0})=1$ . For $b_{0}\in B$ , let $\psi_{b_{0}}$ be such that $\widehat{\psi_{b_{0}}}$ is a bump function adapted to

$$ \displaystyle\{|\xi-b_{0}|\lesssim|b_{0}|^{-q}\}, $$

with $\widehat{\psi_{b_{0}}}(b_{0})=1$ . We choose these to be compactly supported as a matter of convenience, so that the $\approx$ ’s in Section 1.5.1 all become $=$ ’s, but this isn’t really necessary. By the separation assumptions on $A$ and $B$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{a_{0}}|_{A}=1_{\cdot=a_{0}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\widehat{\psi_{b_{0}}}|_{B}=1_{\cdot=b_{0}}. $$

Let $P\colon\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)\to\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ be given by

$$ \displaystyle P(\alpha,\beta)=\sum_{a_{0}\in A}\alpha(a_{0})\varphi_{a_{0}}+\sum_{b_{0}\in B}\beta(b_{0})\psi_{b_{0}}. $$

We want to show that the series

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(1-\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P)^{j} $$

converges strongly in the space of continuous linear operators on $\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ . We will do this by proving an operator norm estimate of the form

$$ \displaystyle\|(1-\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P)(\alpha,\beta)\|\lesssim o_{\delta\to\infty}(1)\|(\alpha,\beta)\| $$

for a countable family of norms which generate the Fréchet topology on $\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ . Here it is crucial that the constant and decay rate $o_{\delta\to\infty}(1)$ are uniform for all norms in the family. Then for $\delta$ sufficiently large,

$$ \displaystyle\|(1-\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P)(\alpha,\beta)\|\leq\frac{1}{2}\|(\alpha,\beta)\| $$

for all norms, and the series (2.2) converges as desired. This uniformity fails for the most obvious family of norms, so we need to be careful in which norms we use. Our next step is to describe these norms.

Given a weight function $w\colon[1,\infty)\to\mathbf{R}^{+}$ and an exponent $r>0$ , define

$$ \displaystyle\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{r}(A)}=\sum_{a\in A}|\alpha(a)|w(|a|^{r}) $$

for $\alpha\in\mathcal{S}(A)$ , and define $\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{r}(B)}$ for $\beta\in\mathcal{S}(B)$ analogously. These are weighted $\ell^{1}$ norms. Recall $|a|,|b|\geq 1$ for $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ , so $w(|a|^{r})$ and $w(|b|^{r})$ are defined.

Since we are in the subcritical case $pq<1$ , we can choose $\tilde{p}>p$ and $\tilde{q}>q$ with $\tilde{p}\tilde{q}=1$ (on a first reading, we suggest that the reader focus on the case $p,q<1$ and $\tilde{p}=\tilde{q}=1$ ). Fix some $s_{0}>0$ large depending on $\tilde{p},\tilde{q}$ , to be chosen later. For the remainder of Section 2, all constants will be allowed to depend implicitly on $\tilde{p},\tilde{q},s_{0}$ , in addition to $p,q,d$ . For $s>s_{0}$ , let $w_{s}$ be the weight function

$$ \displaystyle w_{s}(t)=\max\{t^{s_{0}},c_{s}t^{s}\}, $$

where $c_{s}>0$ is a constant which is small depending on $s$ . The freedom to choose $c_{s}$ small allows us to ensure that $w_{s}(t)$ will not start growing like $t^{s}$ until $t$ is as large as we like. On the other hand, $w_{s}(t)$ at least grows like $t^{s_{0}}$ , so

$$ \displaystyle w_{s}(t^{1+\gamma})\geq t^{s_{0}\gamma}w_{s}(t) $$

for any $\gamma>0$ . For $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ , let

$$ \displaystyle\|(\alpha,\beta)\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)}=\|\alpha\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)}+\|\beta\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)} $$

(although this looks complicated, it simplifies in the model case $\tilde{p}=\tilde{q}=1$ because the exponents $\tilde{p},\tilde{q}$ don’t affect the definition of the norm). This family of norms on $\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ , ranging over $s>s_{0}$ , generates the topology on $\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ , and along this family we will have uniformity in (2.3). The following proposition is the key estimate.

#### Proposition 2.1.

One has the bounds

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}|_{B}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)}\lesssim\delta^{-1}w_{s}(|a_{0}|^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\psi_{b_{0}}|_{A}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)}\lesssim\delta^{-1}w_{s}(|b_{0}|^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}) $$

uniformly in $s>s_{0}$ .

The factor $\delta^{-1}$ is not sharp, but all we need is that it goes to zero at a rate independent of $s$ as $\delta\to\infty$ .

#### Proof.

We only prove the first inequality, as the second is completely analogous. Write

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{a_{0}}(x)=\varphi(|a_{0}|^{p}(x-a_{0})) $$

with $\varphi$ a standard bump function. Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}|_{B}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}}=\sum_{b\in B}|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}(b)|w_{s}(|b|^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}})=|a_{0}|^{-pd}\sum_{b\in B}|\widehat{\varphi}(|a_{0}|^{-p}b)|w_{s}(|b|^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}). $$

Let $\varepsilon>0$ be such that $\tilde{p}=p+2\varepsilon$ . We drop the factor of $|a_{0}|^{-pd}\leq 1$ , and split the sum based on whether $|b|$ is smaller or bigger than $|a_{0}|^{p+\varepsilon}$ . When $|b|$ is bigger, the Schwartz decay of $\widehat{\varphi}$ kicks in. Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}|_{B}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}}\lesssim\underbrace{\sum_{|b|\leq|a_{0}|^{p+\varepsilon}}w_{s}(|b|^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}})}_{\mbox{{I}}}+\underbrace{\sum_{|b|>|a_{0}|^{p+\varepsilon}}\min\{(|a_{0}|^{-p}|b|)^{-s_{0}^{\prime}},O_{s}(|a_{0}|^{-p}|b|)^{-s^{\prime}}\}w_{s}(|b|^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}})}_{\mbox{{II}}}, $$

where we choose $s_{0}^{\prime},s^{\prime}$ large depending on $s_{0},s$ , respectively.

For $|b|\leq|a_{0}|^{p+\varepsilon}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|b|^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}\leq|a_{0}|^{(p+\varepsilon)\tilde{q}^{1/2}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad(p+\varepsilon)\tilde{q}^{1/2}<\tilde{p}\tilde{q}^{1/2}=\tilde{p}^{1/2}, $$

so by (2.4) and the fact that there are only polynomially many $b$ ’s in the sum,

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{{I}}\lesssim|a_{0}|^{-(s_{1}-O(1))}w_{s}(|a_{0}|^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}})\qquad\text{for some}\qquad s_{1}\gtrsim s_{0}. $$

Since $s_{0}$ is large, the exponent $s_{1}-O(1)$ can be taken to be at least $1/\varpi$ . Combined with $|a_{0}|\gtrsim\delta^{\varpi}$ (which we arranged at the beginning of this section), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{{I}}\lesssim\delta^{-1}w_{s}(|a_{0}|^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}). $$

The summand in II is a product of a min and a max (because $w_{s}$ is a max of two quantities). Estimating this product in two different ways based on which argument of the max is bigger,

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{{II}}\lesssim\sum_{|b|>|a_{0}|^{p+\varepsilon}}(|a_{0}|^{-p}|b|)^{-s_{0}^{\prime}}|b|^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}s_{0}}+\sum_{|b|>|a_{0}|^{p+\varepsilon}}O_{s}(|a_{0}|^{-p}|b|)^{-s^{\prime}}c_{s}|b|^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}s}. $$

Taking $s_{0}^{\prime},s^{\prime}$ large enough, and taking $c_{s}$ small enough to cancel out the implied constant, a dyadic decomposition in $|b|$ easily yields

$$ \displaystyle\mbox{{II}}\lesssim|a_{0}|^{-1/\varpi}\lesssim\delta^{-1}\leq\delta^{-1}w_{s}(|a_{0}|^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}). $$

Hence

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}|_{B}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}} \displaystyle\lesssim\mbox{{I}}+\mbox{{II}}\lesssim\delta^{-1}w_{s}(|a_{0}|^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}).\qed $$

Now fix $\delta$ to be at least $2$ times the implied constants in Proposition 2.1. Then by (2.1) and the proposition,

$$ \displaystyle\|(1-\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P)(1_{\cdot=a_{0}},0)\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|(1_{\cdot=a_{0}},0)\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)} $$

and similarly

$$ \displaystyle\|(1-\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P)(0,1_{\cdot=b_{0}})\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|(0,1_{\cdot=b_{0}})\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)}. $$

Thus by the definition of the norm and the triangle inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\|(1-\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P)(\alpha,\beta)\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|(\alpha,\beta)\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w_{s}}^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}(B)} $$

for all $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ . Hence the power series

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(1-\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P)^{j} $$

converges in operator norm with respect to the norm associated to $s$ , for all $s>s_{0}$ . In particular, it converges strongly, and defines an operator on $\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ which inverts $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P$ . It follows that $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ is surjective, as desired.

### 2.2. Completing the proof of Theorem 1.3

Now suppose $\delta$ is arbitrary. We wish to show that $\Coker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ has dimension $O_{\delta}(1)$ , and $\Ker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ is infinite-dimensional.

To prove the former, remove $O_{\delta}(1)$ points from $A,B$ to form subsets $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ and $B^{\prime}\subseteq B$ which are $(p^{\prime},\delta^{\prime})$ -separated and $(q^{\prime},\delta^{\prime})$ -separated, respectively, for fixed $p^{\prime}>p$ and $q^{\prime}>q$ with $p^{\prime}q^{\prime}<1$ , and for $\delta^{\prime}$ sufficiently large depending on $p^{\prime},q^{\prime}$ . Then $\mathcal{F}_{A^{\prime},B^{\prime}}$ is surjective by the argument above, so it follows immediately that $\dim\Coker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}=O_{\delta}(1)$ .

To prove the latter, add infinitely many points to $A,B$ to form supersets $A^{\prime}\supseteq A$ and $B^{\prime}\supseteq B$ which are $(p,\delta^{\prime})$ -separated and $(q,\delta^{\prime})$ -separated, respectively, for some $\delta^{\prime}\gtrsim\delta$ . The subspace of $\mathcal{S}(A^{\prime})\oplus\mathcal{S}(B^{\prime})$ consisting of sequences which vanish on $A$ and $B$ is infinite-dimensional. Since $\Coker\mathcal{F}_{A^{\prime},B^{\prime}}$ is finite-dimensional, this subspace must meet $\im\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{B}^{\prime}}$ in an infinite-dimensional subspace $\mathcal{E}$ . The preimage of $\mathcal{E}$ under $\mathcal{F}_{A^{\prime},B^{\prime}}$ is an infinite-dimensional subspace of $\Ker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ .

## 3. Sparse critical case: proof of Theorem 1.5

We follow the outline in Section 1.5.2. By the same idea as in the last paragraph of Section 2.2, it suffices to show that the image of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ contains all finitely supported sequences.

As in Section 2.1, we may assume all points in $A,B$ have magnitude $\gtrsim\delta^{\varpi}$ (with $\varpi\gtrsim 1$ ), in particular $\geq 1$ because $\delta$ is large.

Let $\rho\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ be such that $\hat{\rho}$ is a standard bump function and $\rho(0)=1$ . Furthermore, take $\hat{\rho}$ to be Gevrey, so $\rho$ satisfies the quasi-exponential decay condition

$$ \displaystyle|\rho(x)|\lesssim e^{-|x|^{0.9}}. $$

Set

$$ \displaystyle\varphi_{a_{0}}=\rho(\delta^{-1/2}|a_{0}|^{p}(\cdot-a_{0}))\qquad\text{and}\qquad\psi_{b_{0}}=\rho(\delta^{-1/2}|b_{0}|^{q}(\cdot-b_{0}))^{\vee}. $$

Define $P\colon\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)\to\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ by

$$ \displaystyle P(\alpha,\beta)=\sum_{a_{0}\in A}\alpha(a_{0})\varphi_{a_{0}}+\sum_{b_{0}\in B}\beta(b_{0})\psi_{b_{0}} $$

as in the subcritical case.

Let $w\colon[1,\infty)\to\mathbf{R}^{+}$ be the weight function

$$ \displaystyle w(t)=e^{\log^{3}t}. $$

There’s a lot of freedom in how to choose $w$ — it just has to grow faster than $e^{C\log^{2}t}$ and slower than $e^{t^{c}}$ for $C$ a large constant and $c$ a small constant. In analogy with (2.4), we will use that $w$ grows fast enough that

$$ \displaystyle w(2t)\gtrsim_{j}t^{j}w(t) $$

for any $j$ . On the other hand, $w$ grows much slower than the decay rate (3.1) of $\rho$ .

We will show that all sequences in $\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}(B)$ lie in the image of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ , where $\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}(B)$ is the space of $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ for which the norm

$$ \displaystyle\|(\alpha,\beta)\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}(B)}=\sum_{a\in A}|\alpha(a)|w(|a|^{p^{1/2}})+\sum_{b\in B}|\beta(b)|w(|b|^{q^{1/2}}) $$

is finite. This space is what we called $\mathcal{T}(A,B)$ in Section 1.5.2. Of course, this contains all finitely supported sequences $(\alpha,\beta)$ .

To show $\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}(B)\subseteq\im\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ , it suffices as in Section 2.1 to establish the operator norm bound

$$ \displaystyle\|(1-\mathcal{F}_{A,B}P)(\alpha,\beta)\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}(B)}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|(\alpha,\beta)\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}(B)}. $$

By the triangle inequality and the definition of the norm (3.4), this bound follows from the estimates

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi_{a_{0}}|_{A}-1_{\cdot=a_{0}}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}}\leq\frac{1}{4}w(|a_{0}|^{p^{1/2}}), \displaystyle\|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}|_{B}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}}\leq\frac{1}{4}w(|a_{0}|^{p^{1/2}}), \displaystyle\|\psi_{b_{0}}|_{A}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}}\leq\frac{1}{4}w(|b_{0}|^{q^{1/2}}), \displaystyle\|\widehat{\psi_{b_{0}}}|_{B}-1_{\cdot=b_{0}}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}}\leq\frac{1}{4}w(|b_{0}|^{q^{1/2}}), $$

for all $a_{0}\in A$ and $b_{0}\in B$ . So we have reduced the proof of Theorem 1.5 to the four estimates (3.5), (3.6), (3.7), and (3.8).

We begin with (3.5). By definition,

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi_{a_{0}}|_{A}-1_{\cdot=a_{0}}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}}=\sum_{a\neq a_{0}}|\rho(\delta^{-1/2}|a_{0}|^{p}(a-a_{0}))|w(|a|^{p^{1/2}}). $$

The fast decay (3.1) of $\rho$ relative to the much slower growth of $w$ , combined with the $(p,\delta)$ -separation of $A$ , gives us that this sum is dominated by the terms where $a$ is as close as possible to $a_{0}$ , i.e., where $|a-a_{0}|\sim\delta|a_{0}|^{-p}$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi_{a_{0}}|_{A}-1_{\cdot=a_{0}}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}}\lesssim e^{-(\delta^{1/2})^{0.9}}w((|a_{0}|+O(\delta|a_{0}|^{-p}))^{p^{1/2}}). $$

If $|a_{0}|$ is bigger than a large power of $\delta$ , then

$$ \displaystyle w((|a_{0}|+O(\delta|a_{0}|^{-p}))^{p^{1/2}})\leq w((|a_{0}|+1)^{p^{1/2}})\sim w(|a_{0}|^{p^{1/2}}), $$

while if $|a_{0}|\lesssim\delta^{O(1)}$ , then

$$ \displaystyle w((|a_{0}|+O(\delta|a_{0}|^{-p}))^{p^{1/2}})\leq w(\delta^{O(1)})\leq w(\delta^{O(1)})w(|a_{0}|^{p^{1/2}}). $$

In both cases, it follows that

$$ \displaystyle\|\varphi_{a_{0}}|_{A}-1_{\cdot=a_{0}}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{p^{1/2}}}\lesssim e^{-(\delta^{1/2})^{0.8}}w(|a_{0}|^{p^{1/2}}). $$

Taking $\delta$ sufficiently large (independent of $a_{0}$ ), we obtain (3.5). The same argument proves (3.8).

For (3.6), write

$$ \displaystyle|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}(\xi)|=\delta^{d/2}|a_{0}|^{-pd}|\hat{\rho}(\delta^{1/2}|a_{0}|^{-p}\xi)|. $$

Since $\hat{\rho}$ has compact support, $\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}$ is supported on $\{|\xi|\lesssim\delta^{-1/2}|a_{0}|^{p}\}$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}|_{B}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}}=\sum_{b\in B}|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}(b)|w(|b|^{q^{1/2}})\lesssim|a_{0}|^{O(1)}w(O(\delta^{-1/2}|a_{0}|^{p})^{q^{1/2}})=|a_{0}|^{O(1)}w(O(\delta^{-q^{1/2}/2}|a_{0}|^{p^{1/2}})), $$

where in the last equality we have used that $pq=1$ . Taking $\delta$ sufficiently large, we get

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}|_{B}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}}\lesssim|a_{0}|^{O(1)}w\Big(\frac{1}{2}|a_{0}|^{p^{1/2}}\Big). $$

Using (3.3), we can control this by

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\varphi_{a_{0}}}|_{B}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{w}^{q^{1/2}}}\lesssim|a_{0}|^{-1}w(|a_{0}|^{p^{1/2}}). $$

Since $|a_{0}|\gtrsim\delta^{\varpi}$ , we obtain (3.6) when $\delta$ is large. Once again, the same argument gives the analogous estimate (3.7) for $\psi$ .

We have now established (3.5), (3.6), (3.7), (3.8), so the proof of Theorem 1.5 is complete.

## 4. Supercritical case: proof of Theorem 1.4

Sections 4.1 and 4.2 prepare us for Section 4.3, where we implement the strategy in Section 1.5.3. The proof is finished off in Section 4.4, which is quite similar to Section 2.2 in the subcritical case.

### 4.1. Integration by sampling

We are concerned with the following natural question: how best to estimate the integral of a function, knowing only its values on a given discrete sample set? Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2 provide partial answers.

In this section alone, we include in our notation the dependence of constants on $p,d$ .

#### Lemma 4.1.

Fix $k\in\mathbf{Z}^{+}$ , and let $\varepsilon>0$ be sufficiently small depending on $k$ and $d$ . Suppose $E$ is an $\varepsilon r$ -dense subset of a cube $Q\subseteq\mathbf{R}^{d}$ of sidelength $r$ . Then there is a signed measure $\mu$ supported on $E$ of total variation $\|\mu\|\lesssim_{k,d}r^{d}$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{Q}\varphi=\int\varphi\,\textnormal{d}\mu+O_{k,d}(r^{d+k}\|\nabla^{k}\varphi\|_{\infty}) $$

for all $\varphi\in C^{k}(Q)$ .

#### Proof.

By translation invariance and rescaling, we may assume $Q=[0,1]^{d}$ and $r=1$ . We approximate $\varphi$ by its $(k-1)$ -jet at $0$ :

$$ \displaystyle\varphi(x)=J_{0}^{(k-1)}\varphi(x)+O_{k,d}(\|\nabla^{k}\varphi\|_{\infty}),\qquad\text{where}\qquad J_{0}^{(k-1)}\varphi(x)=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k-1}\frac{1}{\alpha!}\partial^{\alpha}\varphi(0)x^{\alpha}. $$

This jet is an element of $\mathcal{P}$ , the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $k-1$ in $d$ variables. Denote $N=\dim\mathcal{P}\lesssim_{k,d}1$ . Fix $N$ points in $[0,1]^{d}$ such that only the zero polynomial in $\mathcal{P}$ vanishes at all $N$ points. Assuming $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small depending on $k$ and $d$ , we can approximate these $N$ points by $x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\in E$ , with the approximation good enough that the bound

$$ \displaystyle\|P\|_{\mathcal{P}}\lesssim_{k,d}\sum_{j=1}^{N}|P(x_{j})| $$

holds for all $P\in\mathcal{P}$ (here $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{P}}$ is some fixed choice of norm on $\mathcal{P}$ ). Let $\mu$ be the unique measure supported on $\{x_{1},\dots,x_{N}\}$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{[0,1]^{d}}P=\int P\,\textnormal{d}\mu $$

for all $P\in\mathcal{P}$ . It follows from (4.3) that $\mu$ has total variation $O_{k,d}(1)$ . Integrating the Taylor approximation (4.2) and applying (4.4), we conclude that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{[0,1]^{d}}\varphi=\int\varphi\,\textnormal{d}\mu+O_{k,d}(\|\nabla^{k}\varphi\|_{\infty}).\qed $$

Let $M_{1}^{\infty}$ be the “unit scale $L^{\infty}$ maximal operator”

$$ \displaystyle M_{1}^{\infty}f(x)=\|f\|_{L^{\infty}(B_{1}(x))}. $$

#### Lemma 4.2.

Fix $k\in\mathbf{Z}^{+}$ . Let $A\subseteq\mathbf{R}^{d}$ be $(p,\delta)$ -dense with $p\geq 0$ and $\delta$ small depending on $k,p,d$ . Then there is a signed measure $\mu$ supported on $A$ , with total variation $O_{k,p,d}(1)$ on each unit ball in $\mathbf{R}^{d}$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}f=\int f\,\textnormal{d}\mu+O_{k,p,d}\Big(\delta^{k}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}M_{1}^{\infty}[\nabla^{k}f](x)\langle x\rangle^{-pk}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big) $$

for all Schwartz functions $f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ .

This could be sharpened by allowing the scale $1$ in $M_{1}^{\infty}$ to decrease as $|x|\to\infty$ , but that would only make a difference if the graph of $|\nabla^{k}f|$ had isolated spikes of width $\lll 1$ , which doesn’t occur in our application. Similarly, the total variation of $\mu$ can be controlled on smaller balls when the center of the ball is far from the origin, but this isn’t necessary for us.

#### Proof.

Partition $\mathbf{R}^{d}$ into dyadic cubes so that the cube $Q_{x}$ containing $x$ has sidelength $\sim_{p,d}C\delta\langle x\rangle^{-p}$ for all $x\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ , where $C\gg_{k,p,d}1$ is a fixed constant. Then $A$ will be dense enough on each cube that Lemma 4.1 applies. Let $\mu$ be the sum of the resulting measures on each cube. Then (4.5) follows by summing (4.1) over the cubes (here it’s important for $\delta$ to be small enough that $Q_{x}\subseteq B_{1}(x)$ for all $x$ , so $M_{1}^{\infty}[\nabla^{k}f](x)$ is an upper bound for $\|\nabla^{k}f\|_{L^{\infty}(Q_{x})}$ ). ∎

### 4.2. The Gabor transform

Fix a standard Schwartz function $\chi\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ with $L^{2}$ norm equal to $1$ . For $y,\eta\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ , denote

$$ \displaystyle\chi_{y,\eta}(x)=\chi(x-y)e^{2\pi i\eta\cdot x}, $$

so $\chi_{y,\eta}$ is a wave packet adapted to $B_{1}(y)\times B_{1}(\eta)$ in phase space. The Gabor transform $Tf$ of a tempered distribution $f\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ is

$$ \displaystyle Tf(y,\eta)=\langle f,\chi_{y,\eta}\rangle=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}f(x)\overline{\chi_{y,\eta}(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x $$

(typically $\chi$ is chosen to be a Gaussian, but all we need is that $\chi$ is Schwartz, so we prefer to leave it unspecified) [5, 16]. Heuristically, this measures the extent to which $f|_{B_{O(1)}(y)}$ oscillates at frequencies $\eta+O(1)$ . When $f$ is Schwartz, $Tf(y,\eta)$ decays faster than any polynomial in $y,\eta$ . For $f$ a general tempered distribution, $Tf(y,\eta)$ grows at most polynomially in $y,\eta$ . The Gabor inversion formula recovers $f$ from $Tf$ , expressing $f$ as an integral linear combination of the wave packets $\chi_{y,\eta}$ . Such an expression is not unique, but it is essentially unique at scales $\gg 1$ , because $\chi_{y,\eta}$ is almost orthogonal to $\chi_{y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}$ when $|y-y^{\prime}|\gg 1$ or $|\eta-\eta^{\prime}|\gg 1$ .

#### Proposition 4.3 (Gabor inversion formula).

For all Schwartz functions $f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle f=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}Tf(y,\eta)\chi_{y,\eta}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta. $$

This holds more generally for tempered distributions when interpreted in the obvious way (i.e., as a Gelfand–Pettis integral).

This is well-known, but the proof is only a few lines, so we include it for the reader’s convenience.

#### Proof.

It suffices to prove this for Schwartz functions, since it will then extend to tempered distributions by continuity. Integrating in $\eta$ first,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}Tf(y,\eta)\chi_{y,\eta}(x)\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\chi(x-y)Tf(y,\cdot)^{\vee}(x)\,\textnormal{d}y. $$

We can write

$$ \displaystyle Tf(y,\eta)=\widehat{\overline{\chi}(\cdot-y)f(\cdot)}(\eta). $$

Thus by Fourier inversion,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}Tf(y,\eta)\chi_{y,\eta}(x)\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}|\chi(x-y)|^{2}f(x)\,\textnormal{d}y=f(x). $$

The last equality is because $\|\chi\|_{L^{2}}=1$ . ∎

For $s\in\mathbf{R}$ , let $\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ be the Banach space consisting of tempered distributions $f\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ for which the norm

$$ \displaystyle\|f\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}|Tf(y,\eta)|\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta $$

is finite. Schwartz functions are dense in $\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ . The inclusions $\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ are continuous. By integration by parts, one can easily check that

$$ \displaystyle\|\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}\lesssim_{s}\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|\widehat{\chi_{y,\eta}}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}\lesssim_{s}\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}. $$

From the latter and the Gabor inversion formula, it follows that the Fourier transform acts as a bounded operator on $\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ .

### 4.3. Injectivity of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$

We execute the argument outlined in Section 1.5.3.

Fix $0<\tilde{p}<p$ and $0<\tilde{q}<q$ with $\tilde{p}\tilde{q}=1$ . On a first reading, we recommend that the reader takes $p,q>1$ and $\tilde{p}=\tilde{q}=1$ . For the remainder of this section, all constants will be allowed to depend implicitly on $\tilde{p},\tilde{q}$ , in addition to $p,q,d$ . Let $k$ be large, to be chosen later. Taking $\delta$ sufficiently small depending on $k$ , there are measures $\mu_{A},\mu_{B}$ supported on $A,B$ as in Lemma 4.2. For $y,\eta\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ , let

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{y,\eta}=\begin{cases}\chi_{y,\eta}\mu_{A}&\mbox{if }\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}},\\
(\widehat{\chi_{y,\eta}}\mu_{B})^{\vee}&\mbox{if }\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}<\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}.\end{cases} $$

Then $\nu_{y,\eta}$ is either a tempered measure on $A$ or the inverse Fourier transform of a tempered measure on $B$ , so $\nu_{y,\eta}\in\mathcal{M}_{A,B}$ (recall $\mathcal{M}_{A,B}$ was defined in Section 1.5.3).

We remark that the inequalities $\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}$ and $\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}<\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}$ are written in the most symmetric way possible, but what we’ll actually use are the equivalent inequalities

$$ \displaystyle\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}\iff\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}<\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}\iff\langle y\rangle<\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}}; $$

these equivalences are where we need $\tilde{p}\tilde{q}=1$ .

#### Proposition 4.4.

Assume $s$ is sufficiently large, $k$ is sufficiently large depending on $s$ , and $\delta$ is sufficiently small depending on $k,s$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}. $$

#### Proof.

We first consider the case $\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}$ , so $\nu_{y,\eta}=\chi_{y,\eta}\mu_{A}$ . To estimate $\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}$ , we want pointwise control on $T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)$ . The trivial bound, using the triangle inequality and the fact that $\mu_{A}$ has total variation $O_{k}(1)$ on unit balls, is

$$ \displaystyle|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|\leq|T\nu_{y,\eta}(z,\zeta)|+|T\chi_{y,\eta}(z,\zeta)|\lesssim_{k}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

When $\zeta$ is not too large, we can do better ( $\eta$ is not too large because $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}}$ ). By (4.5),

$$ \displaystyle|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)| \displaystyle=\Big|\int\chi_{y,\eta}\overline{\chi_{z,\zeta}}\,\textnormal{d}\mu_{A}-\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\chi_{y,\eta}\overline{\chi_{z,\zeta}}\Big| \displaystyle\lesssim_{k}\delta^{k}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}M_{1}^{\infty}[\nabla^{k}(\chi_{y,\eta}\overline{\chi_{z,\zeta}})](x)\langle x\rangle^{-pk}\,\textnormal{d}x \displaystyle\lesssim_{k}\delta^{k}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\max\{\langle\eta\rangle,\langle\zeta\rangle\}^{k}\langle y\rangle^{-pk}. $$

Write $p=\tilde{p}+2\varepsilon$ , and suppose $\langle\zeta\rangle\lesssim\delta^{-1/2}\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}+\varepsilon}$ (this is our condition that $\zeta$ is not too large). Then

$$ \displaystyle\max\{\langle\eta\rangle,\langle\zeta\rangle\}\lesssim\delta^{-1/2}\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}+\varepsilon}=\delta^{-1/2}\langle y\rangle^{p-\varepsilon}. $$

We thus obtain

$$ \displaystyle|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|\lesssim_{k}\delta^{k/2}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\langle y\rangle^{-k\varepsilon}. $$

Combining this with the trivial bound (4.9) for large $\zeta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}} \displaystyle\lesssim_{k}\int_{\{(z,\zeta):\langle\zeta\rangle\lesssim\delta^{-1/2}\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}+\varepsilon}\}}\delta^{k/2}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\langle y\rangle^{-k\varepsilon}\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta \displaystyle\qquad+\int_{\{(z,\zeta):\langle\zeta\rangle\gtrsim\delta^{-1/2}\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}+\varepsilon}\}}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta \displaystyle\lesssim_{k,s}\delta^{k/2}\langle y\rangle^{-s-k\varepsilon}+\langle y\rangle^{-s}(\delta^{-1/2}\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}+\varepsilon})^{-(s-d)}. $$

Since $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}}$ , we can estimate the right hand side by

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}\lesssim_{k,s}[\delta^{k/2}\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}s-k\varepsilon}+\delta^{(s-d)/2}\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}d-\varepsilon(s-d)}]\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}. $$

Taking $s$ sufficiently large, $k$ sufficiently large depending on $s$ , and $\delta$ sufficiently small depending on $k,s$ , we obtain the desired bound (4.8) in the case $\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}$ .

In the other case $\langle y\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}<\langle\eta\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}$ , write

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}=\|(\widehat{\chi_{y,\eta}}\mu_{B}-\widehat{\chi_{y,\eta}})^{\vee}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}\lesssim_{s}\|\widehat{\chi_{y,\eta}}\mu_{B}-\widehat{\chi_{y,\eta}}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}. $$

The Fourier transform $\widehat{\chi_{y,\eta}}$ is a wave packet adapted to $B_{1}(y^{\prime})\times B_{1}(\eta^{\prime})$ in phase space, where $(y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})=(\eta,-y)$ . Now $\langle y^{\prime}\rangle^{\tilde{q}^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta^{\prime}\rangle^{\tilde{p}^{1/2}}$ and $B$ is $(q,\delta)$ -dense, so we can apply the same argument as in the first case (but with $p,q$ swapped and $\tilde{p},\tilde{q}$ swapped) to estimate the right hand side of (4.10). ∎

Take $s,k,\delta$ to be as in Proposition 4.4, so (4.8) holds. Define $P\colon\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})\to\mathcal{M}_{A,B}$ by

$$ \displaystyle Pf=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}Tf(y,\eta)\nu_{y,\eta}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta. $$

This is our parametrix. By Gabor inversion and (4.8),

$$ \displaystyle\|(1-P)f\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\|f\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}} $$

for all $f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ . Therefore $P$ extends continuously to a bounded linear operator on $\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ , and the power series

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(1-P)^{j} $$

converges in operator norm. This series inverts $P$ , so $P$ surjects onto $\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ . But $P$ maps into $\mathcal{M}_{A,B}$ , so we must have $\mathcal{M}_{A,B}\supseteq\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ , and hence $\mathcal{M}_{A,B}=\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ because $\mathcal{M}_{A,B}$ is closed and $\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ is dense. We conclude by duality that $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ is injective.

### 4.4. Completing the proof of Theorem 1.4

Suppose now that $\delta$ is arbitrary. We must show that $\Ker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ has dimension $O_{\delta}(1)$ , and $\Coker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ is infinite-dimensional. This is very similar to Section 2.2.

To prove the first statement, add $O_{\delta}(1)$ points to $A,B$ to form supersets $A^{\prime}\supseteq A$ and $B^{\prime}\supseteq B$ which are $(p^{\prime},\delta^{\prime})$ -dense and $(q^{\prime},\delta^{\prime})$ -dense, respectively, for fixed $p^{\prime}<p$ and $q^{\prime}<q$ with $p^{\prime}q^{\prime}>1$ , and for $\delta^{\prime}$ sufficiently small depending on $p^{\prime},q^{\prime}$ . Then $\mathcal{F}_{A^{\prime},B^{\prime}}$ is injective by our work so far. It follows directly that $\dim\Ker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}=O_{\delta}(1)$ .

To prove the second statement, remove infinitely many points from $A,B$ to form subsets $A^{\prime}\subseteq A$ and $B^{\prime}\subseteq B$ which are $(p,\delta^{\prime})$ -dense and $(q,\delta^{\prime})$ -dense, respectively, for some $\delta^{\prime}\lesssim\delta$ . The subspace of $\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ consisting of sequences which vanish on $A^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime}$ is infinite-dimensional. Since $\Ker\mathcal{F}_{A^{\prime},B^{\prime}}$ is finite-dimensional, the image of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ must have finite-dimensional intersection with this subspace. Therefore the image of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ has infinite codimension in $\mathcal{S}(A)\oplus\mathcal{S}(B)$ , i.e., $\Coker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ is infinite-dimensional.

## 5. Dense critical case: proof of Theorem 1.6

### 5.1. Oscillatory integral estimates

In this section, we carry out the usual integration by parts for oscillatory integrals of the form

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\psi e^{i\phi} $$

with non-stationary phase (i.e., $\nabla\phi\neq 0$ ), paying attention to the dependence on derivatives of $\phi,\psi$ .

Since $\nabla\phi\neq 0$ , we can integrate by parts by writing

$$ \displaystyle\int\psi e^{i\phi}=\frac{1}{i}\int\psi\frac{\nabla\phi}{|\nabla\phi|^{2}}\cdot\nabla e^{i\phi}=i\int\Div\Big(\psi\frac{\nabla\phi}{|\nabla\phi|^{2}}\Big)e^{i\phi}. $$

Let $\mathcal{D}_{\phi}$ denote the differential operator

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\phi}\psi=i\Div\Big(\psi\frac{\nabla\phi}{|\nabla\phi|^{2}}\Big). $$

Iterating the above,

$$ \displaystyle\int\psi e^{i\phi}=\int(\mathcal{D}_{\phi}^{n}\psi)e^{i\phi} $$

for any $n\in\mathbf{N}$ . We now want to estimate $\mathcal{D}_{\phi}^{n}\psi$ .

#### Lemma 5.1.

One has the pointwise bound

$$ \displaystyle|\mathcal{D}_{\phi}^{n}\psi|\lesssim_{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{1}{|\nabla\phi|^{n+k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j_{1},\dots,j_{k}\geq 2\\
j_{1}+\cdots+j_{k}\leq n+k\end{subarray}}|\nabla^{j_{1}}\phi|\cdots|\nabla^{j_{k}}\phi||\nabla^{n+k-j_{1}-\cdots-j_{k}}\psi| $$

(when $k=0$ we take the inner sum to be equal to $|\nabla^{n}\psi|$ ).

#### Proof.

This could easily be proven by induction. Instead we give a proof which suggests how to guess the right hand side.

By the product and quotient rules, $\mathcal{D}_{\phi}^{n}\psi$ is a linear combination of terms of the form

$$ \displaystyle\frac{(\partial^{\alpha_{1}}\phi)\cdots(\partial^{\alpha_{k}}\phi)}{|\nabla\phi|^{\ell}}\partial^{\beta}\psi $$

for some $k,\ell\in\mathbf{N}$ and multiindices $\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{k},\beta\in\mathbf{N}^{d}$ (here $\ell$ will be even, but we won’t use this for our estimates). By homogeneity considerations, we can constrain these parameters. Suppose $\phi$ is homogeneous of order $r$ . By the product rule, $\mathcal{D}_{\phi}^{n}\psi$ is a linear combination of terms of the form

$$ \displaystyle\partial^{\gamma_{1}}\Big(\frac{\partial_{i_{1}}\phi}{|\nabla\phi|^{2}}\Big)\cdots\partial^{\gamma_{n}}\Big(\frac{\partial_{i_{n}}\phi}{|\nabla\phi|^{2}}\Big)\partial^{\beta}\psi $$

for some indices $i_{1},\dots,i_{n}\in\{1,\dots,d\}$ and multiindices $\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n},\beta\in\mathbf{N}^{d}$ with $|\gamma_{1}|+\cdots+|\gamma_{n}|+|\beta|=n$ . The terms (5.2) come from further expanding this. The part of (5.2) depending on $\phi$ is homogeneous of order

$$ \displaystyle kr-|\alpha_{1}|-\cdots-|\alpha_{k}|-\ell(r-1), $$

while the part of (5.3) depending on $\phi$ is homogeneous of order

$$ \displaystyle n(1-r)-|\gamma_{1}|-\cdots-|\gamma_{n}|=|\beta|-nr. $$

These orders must be equal for all $r$ , so we must have

$$ \displaystyle\ell=n+k\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\beta|=n+k-|\alpha_{1}|-\cdots-|\alpha_{k}|. $$

Denoting $j_{i}=|\alpha_{i}|$ , we conclude that $\mathcal{D}_{\phi}^{n}\psi$ is bounded by a sum of terms of the form

$$ \displaystyle\frac{|\nabla^{j_{1}}\phi|\cdots|\nabla^{j_{k}}\phi|}{|\nabla\phi|^{n+k}}|\nabla^{n+k-j_{1}-\cdots-j_{k}}\psi| $$

with $n+k-j_{1}-\cdots-j_{k}\geq 0$ . We may assume $j_{1},\dots,j_{k}\geq 2$ , as otherwise we can cancel some factors in the numerator and the denominator (and this cancellation doesn’t change the shape of the term). Then the condition $j_{1}+\cdots+j_{k}\leq n+k$ forces $k\leq n$ . This completes the proof. ∎

We give two applications, Corollary 5.2 and Proposition 5.3. The first doesn’t require such precise estimates as Lemma 5.1 gives, but the second does.

#### Corollary 5.2.

Let $M,r>0$ . Suppose $\phi$ obeys the derivative bounds

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)|\gtrsim M\langle x\rangle^{r}\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\nabla^{k}\phi(x)|\lesssim_{k}M\langle x\rangle^{r} $$

for all $k\geq 2$ and $x\in\supp\psi$ . Then for any $n\in\mathbf{N}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\psi e^{i\phi}\Big|\lesssim_{n}M^{-n}\sum_{i=0}^{n}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}|\nabla^{i}\psi(x)|\langle x\rangle^{-rn}\,\textnormal{d}x. $$

#### Proof.

This is immediate from (5.1) and Lemma 5.1. ∎

#### Proposition 5.3.

Let $X\geq 1$ , let $R,V,\lambda,M>0$ with $R\lesssim X$ , and let $r\in\mathbf{R}$ . Suppose $\psi$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla^{k}\psi\|_{L^{1}(\mathbf{R}^{d})}\lesssim_{k}VR^{-k} $$

for all $k\geq 0$ , and $\phi$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)|\gtrsim\lambda\qquad\text{and}\qquad|\nabla^{k}\phi(x)|\lesssim_{k}MX^{r+1-k} $$

for all $k\geq 2$ and $x\in\supp\psi$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\psi e^{i\phi}\Big|\lesssim V\Big\langle\frac{\lambda R}{\langle\lambda^{-1}MRX^{r-1}\rangle}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

The model scenario is when $\psi$ is essentially constant at scales $\ll R$ , the total mass of $\psi$ is $\lesssim V$ , the support of $\psi$ is contained in $\{|x|\sim X\}$ , and $\phi$ is a linear function plus the dot product of $m$ with an $(r+1)$ -pseudohomogeneous diffeomorphism, where $m\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ is a fixed vector of magnitude $\lesssim M$ (e.g. (5.7)).

#### Proof.

The trivial bound is $V$ , so we can remove the outer angle brackets, and we just need to prove that

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\psi e^{i\phi}\Big|\lesssim V\Big(\frac{\langle\lambda^{-1}MRX^{r-1}\rangle}{\lambda R}\Big)^{\infty}. $$

By (5.1), Lemma 5.1, and the assumed derivative bounds,

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int\psi e^{i\phi}\Big|\lesssim_{n}V\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{1}{\lambda^{n+k}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j_{1},\dots,j_{k}\geq 2\\
j_{1}+\cdots+j_{k}\leq n+k\end{subarray}}M^{k}X^{k(r+1)-j_{1}-\cdots-j_{k}}R^{-n-k+j_{1}+\cdots+j_{k}} $$

for any $n\in\mathbf{N}$ . Since $R\lesssim X$ , the inner sum is dominated by the term where $j_{1}+\cdots+j_{k}$ is as small as possible, namely $2k$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int\psi e^{i\phi}\Big| \displaystyle\lesssim_{n}V\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{1}{\lambda^{n+k}}M^{k}X^{k(r-1)}R^{-n+k} \displaystyle=V\Big(\frac{1}{\lambda R}\Big)^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}(\lambda^{-1}MRX^{r-1})^{k} \displaystyle\lesssim_{n}V\Big(\frac{\langle\lambda^{-1}MRX^{r-1}\rangle}{\lambda R}\Big)^{n}.\qed $$

### 5.2. Injectivity of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ : balanced density case

We first prove Theorem 1.6 in the special case where $p=q=1$ , so $A,B$ have comparable density. This allows for some technical simplifications, although the main ideas are the same in the general case.

By composing $\sigma_{A},\sigma_{B}$ with $x\mapsto(-x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{d})$ if necessary, we may assume $\sigma_{A},\sigma_{B}$ are orientation-preserving.

We proceed as in the proof of Theorem 1.4, but instead of using Lemma 4.2 to define $\mu_{A}$ and $\mu_{B}$ , we explicitly put

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{A}=\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\delta^{d}\det D\sigma_{A}(n)\Dirac_{\delta\sigma_{A}(n)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mu_{B}=\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\delta^{d}\det D\sigma_{B}(n)\Dirac_{\delta\sigma_{B}(n)} $$

(we write $\Dirac_{x}$ instead of $\delta_{x}$ for a Dirac mass at $x$ to avoid overloading the symbol $\delta$ ).

#### Lemma 5.4 (Twisted Poisson summation formula).

Let $\sigma\colon\mathbf{R}^{d}\to\mathbf{R}^{d}$ be an orientation-preserving $r$ -pseudohomogeneous diffeomorphism for some $r>0$ . Then for all Schwartz functions $f\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\det D\sigma(n)f(\sigma(n))=\sum_{m\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}f(x)e^{-2\pi im\cdot\sigma^{-1}(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x. $$

The pseudohomogeneity condition could be relaxed — it is only there to ensure that $f\circ\sigma$ is Schwartz.

#### Proof.

By Poisson summation and the change of variables formula,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\det D\sigma(n)f(\sigma(n))=\sum_{m\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\widehat{(\det D\sigma)f\circ\sigma}(m) \displaystyle=\sum_{m\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}f(\sigma(x))e^{-2\pi im\cdot x}\det D\sigma(x)\,\textnormal{d}x \displaystyle=\sum_{m\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}f(x)e^{-2\pi im\cdot\sigma^{-1}(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x.\qed $$

Let

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{y,\eta}=\begin{cases}\chi_{y,\eta}\mu_{A}&\mbox{if }\langle y\rangle\geq\langle\eta\rangle,\\
(\widehat{\chi_{y,\eta}}\mu_{B})^{\vee}&\mbox{if }\langle y\rangle<\langle\eta\rangle.\end{cases} $$

By the same parametrix iteration procedure as in Section 4.3, one deduces injectivity of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ from the following proposition.

#### Proposition 5.5.

Assume $s$ is sufficiently large, and $\delta$ is sufficiently small depending on $s$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}. $$

#### Proof.

First suppose $\langle y\rangle\geq\langle\eta\rangle$ , so $\nu_{y,\eta}=\chi_{y,\eta}\mu_{A}$ . We need pointwise bounds on

$$ \displaystyle|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|=|\langle\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta},\chi_{z,\zeta}\rangle|=\Big|\int\chi_{y,\eta}\overline{\chi_{z,\zeta}}\,\textnormal{d}\mu_{A}-\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\chi_{y,\eta}\overline{\chi_{z,\zeta}}\Big|. $$

When $|\zeta|\gtrsim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+\varepsilon}$ (for fixed $\varepsilon>0$ ), the trivial bound

$$ \displaystyle|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|\lesssim\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty} $$

will suffice, so suppose $|\zeta|\lesssim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+\varepsilon}$ . By Lemma 5.4 and the definition of $\mu_{A}$ , we can rewrite (5.5) as

$$ \displaystyle|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|=\Big|\sum_{0\neq m\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\chi_{y,\eta}(x)\overline{\chi_{z,\zeta}(x)}e^{-2\pi im\cdot\sigma_{A}^{-1}(\delta^{-1}x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|. $$

Rescaling by $\delta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|=\delta^{d}\Big|\sum_{m\neq 0}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\chi_{y,\eta}(\delta x)\overline{\chi_{z,\zeta}(\delta x)}e^{-2\pi im\cdot\sigma_{A}^{-1}(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|. $$

Denote $\tau_{A}=\sigma_{A}^{-1}$ . Then $\tau_{A}$ is $2$ -pseudohomogeneous. Expanding the definitions of $\chi_{y,\eta}$ and $\chi_{z,\zeta}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|=\delta^{d}\Big|\sum_{m\neq 0}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\chi(\delta x-y)\overline{\chi(\delta x-z)}e^{-2\pi i(\delta(\zeta-\eta)\cdot x+m\cdot\tau_{A}(x))}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|. $$

Let

$$ \displaystyle I=\Big|\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\chi(\delta x-y)\overline{\chi(\delta x-z)}e^{-2\pi i\phi(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big| $$

denote the absolute value of the integral, where

$$ \displaystyle\phi(x)=\delta(\zeta-\eta)\cdot x+m\cdot\tau_{A}(x) $$

is the phase. The gradient of the phase is

$$ \displaystyle\nabla\phi(x)=\delta(\zeta-\eta)+D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m. $$

When $|m|\gtrsim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+2\varepsilon}$ , it follows from the pseudohomogeneity bound on $|D\tau_{A}(x)^{-1}|$ and the inequalities $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle$ and $|\zeta|\lesssim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+\varepsilon}$ that the term $D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m$ dominates, so the norm of the gradient of the phase is $\gtrsim|m|\langle x\rangle$ , and non-stationary phase (Corollary 5.2) gives

$$ \displaystyle I\lesssim|m|^{-\infty}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

Suppose instead that $|m|\lesssim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+2\varepsilon}$ . Since $m$ is integral and nonzero, $|m|\geq 1$ , so we must have $|y|\gg\delta^{-0.9}$ (the exponent $0.9$ could be made arbitrarily close to $1$ by decreasing $\varepsilon$ , but this is unnecessary). Now for $x$ near $\delta^{-1}y$ , we can bound $|\nabla\phi(x)|$ below by $|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|$ . By the fundamental theorem of calculus and the $2$ -pseudohomogeneity of $\tau_{A}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)-\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|=|D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m-D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}y)^{T}m|\lesssim|m||x-\delta^{-1}y|. $$

Thus if

$$ \displaystyle|x-\delta^{-1}y|\ll|m|^{-1}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|, $$

then

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)-\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|\ll|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)| $$

and hence

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)|\sim|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|. $$

Using Proposition 5.3 (non-stationary phase) on the region

$$ \displaystyle\{x\in\mathbf{R}^{d}:|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|\text{ and }|x-\delta^{-1}y|\ll|m|^{-1}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|\} $$

with parameters

$$ \displaystyle X \displaystyle=\delta^{-1}|y|, \displaystyle R \displaystyle=\min\{\delta^{-1},|m|^{-1}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|\}, \displaystyle V \displaystyle=\delta^{-d}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}, \displaystyle\lambda \displaystyle=|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|, \displaystyle M \displaystyle=|m|, \displaystyle r \displaystyle=1 $$

(the second argument in the minimum in the definition of $R$ is necessary to capture the derivative bounds of the implicit smooth cutoff to $\{|x-\delta^{-1}y|\ll|m|^{-1}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)|\}$ ), and using the trivial bound on the complementary region, we obtain the estimate

$$ \displaystyle I\lesssim V\Big\langle\frac{\lambda R}{\langle\lambda^{-1}MRX^{r-1}\rangle}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}+\delta^{-d}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\langle\delta|m|^{-1}\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)\rangle^{-\infty}+|y|^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

With our choice of parameters, the second term on the right hand side dominates the other two, so

$$ \displaystyle I\lesssim\delta^{-d}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\langle\delta|m|^{-1}\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}y)\rangle^{-\infty}=\delta^{-d}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\langle\delta^{2}|m|^{-1}(\zeta-\eta+\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}y)^{T}m)\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

We remark that the dual lattice $L^{\vee}$ mentioned in Section 1.5.4 is $\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}y)^{T}\mathbf{Z}^{d}$ .

Combining (5.10), (5.9), and (5.6), we find that

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}} \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}|T(\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{\{(z,\zeta):|\zeta|\lesssim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+\varepsilon}\}}\Big[\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\sum_{0\neq|m|\lesssim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+2\varepsilon}}\langle\delta^{2}|m|^{-1}(\zeta-\eta+\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}y)^{T}m)\rangle^{-\infty} \displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad+\delta^{d}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-\infty}\sum_{|m|\gtrsim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+2\varepsilon}}|m|^{-\infty}\Big]\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta \displaystyle\qquad+\int_{\{(z,\zeta):|\zeta|\gtrsim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+\varepsilon}\}}\langle y-z\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta. $$

When $|y|\lesssim\delta^{-0.9}$ , the first line of the right hand side vanishes, and we get

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}}\lesssim_{s}\delta^{d}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}+\delta^{\varepsilon(s-d)}\langle y\rangle^{-(1+\varepsilon)(s-d)}\langle y\rangle^{-s}. $$

When $|y|\gtrsim\delta^{-0.9}$ , it follows from the $2$ -pseudohomogeneity of $\tau_{A}$ and the fact that $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle$ that

$$ \displaystyle|\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}y)^{T}m-\eta|\sim\delta^{-1}|D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}y)^{T}m|\sim\delta^{-2}|m|\langle y\rangle. $$

Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\chi_{y,\eta}\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}} \displaystyle\lesssim_{s}\sum_{0\neq|m|\lesssim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{1+2\varepsilon}}(\delta^{-2}|m|)^{d}(\delta^{-2}|m|\langle y\rangle)^{-s}\langle y\rangle^{-s}+\delta^{d}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}+\delta^{\varepsilon(s-d)}\langle y\rangle^{-(1+\varepsilon)(s-d)}\langle y\rangle^{-s} \displaystyle\lesssim_{s}\delta^{2(s-d)}\langle y\rangle^{-2s}+\delta^{d}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}+\delta^{\varepsilon(s-d)}\langle y\rangle^{-(2+\varepsilon)s+(1+\varepsilon)d}. $$

In both cases $|y|\lesssim\delta^{-0.9}$ and $|y|\gtrsim\delta^{-0.9}$ , using once again that $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle$ , we conclude the desired bound (5.4) when $s$ is large and $\delta$ is sufficiently small depending on $s$ .

So far we have only considered the situation where $\langle y\rangle\geq\langle\eta\rangle$ . As in the proof of Proposition 4.4 though, the case $\langle y\rangle<\langle\eta\rangle$ reduces to an estimate which is analogous to what we have already shown when $\langle y\rangle\geq\langle\eta\rangle$ . ∎

### 5.3. A variably rescaled Gabor transform

As discussed at the end of Section 1.5.4, for the proof of Theorem 1.6 in general, we need to use a phase space basis $(\rho_{y,\eta})_{y,\eta\in\mathbf{R}^{d}}$ , where $\rho_{y,\eta}$ is a wave packet adapted to $B_{R_{y,\eta}}(y)\times B_{R_{y,\eta}^{-1}}(\eta)$ in phase space, and where we have some flexibility to choose the radii $R_{y,\eta}$ . Proposition 5.7 below describes a modification of the Gabor transform which implements the decomposition of a function in this basis.

A simple case, which we will use in the proof of the proposition, is when $R_{y,\eta}=R$ is constant. Fix an $L^{2}$ -normalized Schwartz function $\chi_{R}$ adapted to the ball $\{|x|\lesssim R\}$ . Let $\chi_{R}$ have $L^{2}$ norm exactly $1$ . For $y,\eta\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ , set

$$ \displaystyle\chi_{R,y,\eta}(x)=\chi_{R}(x-y)e^{2\pi i\eta\cdot x}. $$

Define a rescaled Gabor transform $T_{R}$ in terms of $\chi_{R}$ exactly as in Section 4.2, so

$$ \displaystyle T_{R}f(y,\eta)=\langle f,\chi_{R,y,\eta}\rangle. $$

The proof of the Gabor inversion formula (Proposition 4.3) only depended on $\chi$ having $L^{2}$ norm $1$ , so the same inversion formula holds for $T_{R}$ :

$$ \displaystyle f=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}T_{R}f(y,\eta)\chi_{R,y,\eta}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta. $$

This achieves the goal of decomposing $f$ into wave packets $\chi_{R,y,\eta}$ adapted to $B_{R}(y)\times B_{R^{-1}}(\eta)$ in phase space.

#### Remark 5.6.

In the balanced density case $p=q=1$ , the ordinary Gabor transform was sufficient. This should be viewed as a lucky coincidence. In general, we need to choose $R_{y,\eta}$ carefully when $\langle y\rangle^{p^{1/2}}\sim\langle\eta\rangle^{q^{1/2}}$ , in which case the optimal choice is

$$ \displaystyle R_{y,\eta}\sim\langle y\rangle^{\frac{1-p}{2}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad R_{y,\eta}^{-1}\sim\langle\eta\rangle^{\frac{1-q}{2}} $$

(note $\langle y\rangle^{\frac{1-p}{2}}\langle\eta\rangle^{\frac{1-q}{2}}\sim 1$ because $\langle y\rangle^{p^{1/2}}\sim\langle\eta\rangle^{q^{1/2}}$ and $pq=1$ ). When $p=q=1$ , the right hand sides in (5.12) reduce to $1$ , so the ordinary Gabor transform works.

In the proof of Theorem 1.6, we will take

$$ \displaystyle R_{y,\eta}=\frac{\langle y\rangle^{1/2}}{\langle\eta\rangle^{1/2}} $$

for all $y,\eta\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ . This agrees with (5.12) when $\langle y\rangle^{p^{1/2}}\sim\langle\eta\rangle^{q^{1/2}}$ . One can keep (5.13) in mind as a model example in the proof of Proposition 5.7.

#### Proposition 5.7.

For $y,\eta\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ , let $R_{y,\eta}>0$ satisfy the sublinear growth/decay property

$$ \displaystyle R_{y,\eta}\lesssim\langle y\rangle^{1-\varepsilon}\qquad\text{and}\qquad R_{y,\eta}^{-1}\lesssim\langle\eta\rangle^{1-\varepsilon} $$

( $\varepsilon>0$ fixed), as well as the radial constancy property

$$ \displaystyle R_{y,\eta}\sim R_{y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad\langle y\rangle\sim\langle y^{\prime}\rangle\text{ and }\langle\eta\rangle\sim\langle\eta^{\prime}\rangle. $$

Then there are $L^{2}$ -normalized vector-valued wave packets $\rho_{y,\eta},\tilde{\rho}_{y,\eta}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d};\ell^{2})$ adapted to $B_{R_{y,\eta}}(y)\times B_{R_{y,\eta}^{-1}}(\eta)$ in phase space such that if $\widetilde{T}$ denotes the modified Gabor transform

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{T}f(y,\eta)=\langle f,\tilde{\rho}_{y,\eta}\rangle $$

for scalar-valued $f$ (so $\widetilde{T}f$ is vector-valued), then the inversion formula

$$ \displaystyle f=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}\widetilde{T}f(y,\eta)\cdot\rho_{y,\eta}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta $$

holds.

All of our definitions for scalar-valued functions have obvious analogs for vector-valued functions. For example, the statement that $\rho_{y,\eta}$ is a vector-valued wave packet means that it is of the form (1.6), where $\chi\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d};\ell^{2})$ is a standard vector-valued Schwartz function in the sense that it satisfies the bounds (1.4). Linear operators defined on scalar-valued functions act component-wise on vector-valued functions. The pointwise absolute value of a vector-valued function is its pointwise $\ell^{2}$ norm. From this it is clear how to extend all the usual function space norms, like $\|\cdot\|_{L^{p}(\mathbf{R}^{d})}$ or $\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{S}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})}$ , to the vector-valued setting. Multiplication of scalar-valued functions corresponds to dot product of vector-valued functions, and the inequality $|fg|\leq|f||g|$ for scalar-valued $f,g$ corresponds to Cauchy–Schwarz. Because of all these parallels, vector-valued functions are as nice as scalar-valued functions for our purposes.

The sublinear growth/decay condition on $R_{y,\eta}$ in Proposition 5.7 ensures that $\rho_{y,\eta}$ really is localized near $(y,\eta)$ in phase space. Otherwise the uncertainty principle would make $\rho_{y,\eta}$ indistinguishable from a Schwartz function adapted to a ball in either physical or frequency space (as discussed at the end of Section 1.4.3).

The radial constancy condition could be relaxed to a local constancy condition, but we won’t bother because (5.13) is radial.

#### Proof.

For dyadic numbers $N,M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}$ , let $P_{N,M}$ be the operator acting on functions $f$ on $\mathbf{R}^{d}$ by first applying a Littlewood–Paley projection to frequencies $\{\langle\xi\rangle\sim M\}$ , and then applying the analogous physical space projection to $\{\langle x\rangle\sim N\}$ . Then $P_{N,M}$ is essentially a projection to the region

$$ \displaystyle\{(x,\xi)\in\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}:\langle x\rangle\sim N\text{ and }\langle\xi\rangle\sim M\} $$

in phase space. Since $N,M\gtrsim 1$ , and hence $NM\gtrsim 1$ , this respects the uncertainty principle. We now have a preliminary decomposition

$$ \displaystyle f=\sum_{N,M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}}P_{N,M}f. $$

For each $N,M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}$ , pick some $y_{N},\eta_{M}\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ with $\langle y_{N}\rangle\sim N$ and $\langle\eta_{M}\rangle\sim M$ , and set $R_{N,M}\sim R_{y_{N},\eta_{M}}$ . By the radial constancy property, this is well-defined up to constants. Using the rescaled Gabor inversion formula (5.11), further decompose

$$ \displaystyle f \displaystyle=\sum_{N,M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}T_{R_{N,M}}P_{N,M}f(y,\eta)\chi_{R_{N,M},y,\eta}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta \displaystyle=\sum_{N,M\in 2^{\mathbf{N}}}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}\langle f,P_{N,M}^{\ast}\chi_{R_{N,M},y,\eta}\rangle\chi_{R_{N,M},y,\eta}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta. $$

Note that the adjoint $P_{N,M}^{\ast}$ is still essentially a projection to the region (5.15) in phase space (it acts by projecting in physical space first and then in frequency space). By the sublinear growth/decay property, the essential phase space support of the wave packet $\chi_{R_{N,M},y,\eta}$ is far from (5.15) unless $N\sim\langle y\rangle$ and $M\sim\langle\eta\rangle$ . It follows by routine estimates that we can write

$$ \displaystyle P_{N,M}^{\ast}\chi_{R_{N,M},y,\eta}=c_{y,\eta,N,M}\varphi_{y,\eta,N,M}, $$

where $\varphi_{y,\eta,N,M}$ is an $L^{2}$ -normalized wave packet adapted to $B_{R_{N,M}}(y)\times B_{R_{N,M}^{-1}}(\eta)$ in phase space, and $c_{y,\eta,N,M}\geq 0$ is a constant satisfying

$$ \displaystyle c_{y,\eta,N,M}\lesssim\Delta_{N,\langle y\rangle}^{\infty}\Delta_{M,\langle\eta\rangle}^{\infty}; $$

here we denote

$$ \displaystyle\Delta_{X,Y}=\min\Big\{\frac{X}{Y},\frac{Y}{X}\Big\} $$

(so $c_{y,\eta,N,M}$ is essentially the indicator that $N\sim\langle y\rangle$ and $M\sim\langle\eta\rangle$ ). Let $\rho_{y,\eta},\tilde{\rho}_{y,\eta}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d};\ell^{2}(2^{\mathbf{N}}\times 2^{\mathbf{N}}))$ be the vector-valued functions whose $(N,M)$ components are

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{y,\eta,N,M}=c_{y,\eta,N,M}^{1/2}\chi_{R_{N,M},y,\eta}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tilde{\rho}_{y,\eta,N,M}=c_{y,\eta,N,M}^{-1/2}P_{N,M}^{\ast}\chi_{R_{N,M},y,\eta}. $$

By (5.17) and (5.18), only the $O(1)$ many components where $N\sim\langle y\rangle$ and $M\sim\langle\eta\rangle$ essentially contribute to $\rho_{y,\eta},\tilde{\rho}_{y,\eta}$ . Therefore $\rho_{y,\eta},\tilde{\rho}_{y,\eta}$ are wave packets adapted to $B_{R_{y,\eta}}(y)\times B_{R_{y,\eta}^{-1}}(\eta)$ in phase space, as desired. The inversion formula (5.14) is immediate from (5.16). ∎

Using the transform $\widetilde{T}$ , we define a scale of Banach spaces between $\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ and $\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ as in Section 4.2. Let $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ for $s\in\mathbf{R}$ be the space of tempered distributions $f\in\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ for which the norm

$$ \displaystyle\|f\|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}}=\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}|\widetilde{T}f(y,\eta)|\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta $$

is finite. The inclusions $\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})\hookrightarrow\mathcal{S}^{\prime}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ are continuous and dense.

If $\psi_{y,\eta}$ is an $L^{2}$ -normalized wave packet adapted to $B_{R_{y,\eta}}(y)\times B_{R_{y,\eta}^{-1}}(\eta)$ in phase space, then $\widetilde{T}\psi_{y,\eta}$ is essentially supported on $B_{R_{y,\eta}}(y)\times B_{R_{y,\eta}^{-1}}(\eta)$ , and $\|\widetilde{T}\psi_{y,\eta}\|_{L^{\infty}}\lesssim 1$ . Therefore

$$ \displaystyle\|\psi_{y,\eta}\|_{\widetilde{S}^{-s}}\lesssim_{s}\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}. $$

#### Proposition 5.8.

Let the notation be as above, and suppose in addition that $R_{\eta,-y}\sim R_{y,\eta}^{-1}$ . Then the Fourier transform is bounded on $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ .

Since $R_{\eta,-y}\sim R_{\eta,y}$ by the radial constancy property, we could just as well have written $R_{\eta,y}\sim R_{y,\eta}^{-1}$ . However, this condition comes from the fact that the Fourier transform acts on phase space by $(y,\eta)\mapsto(\eta,-y)$ (see Section 1.4.3), so we feel that writing $R_{\eta,-y}$ is more suggestive.

The hypothesis $R_{\eta,-y}\sim R_{y,\eta}^{-1}$ is satisfied in the main example (5.13).

#### Proof.

By the inversion formula (5.14) and the triangle inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\|\hat{f}\|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}}\leq\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}}|\widetilde{T}f(y,\eta)|\|\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}\|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}}\,\textnormal{d}y\,\textnormal{d}\eta, $$

so it suffices to show that

$$ \displaystyle\|\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}\|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}}\lesssim_{s}\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}. $$

This follows from (5.19), since $\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}$ is an $L^{2}$ -normalized wave packet adapted to $B_{R_{y,\eta}^{-1}}(\eta)\times B_{R_{y,\eta}}(-y)$ in phase space, and $R_{y,\eta}^{-1}\sim R_{\eta,-y}$ . ∎

### 5.4. Injectivity of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ : general case

The strategy is the same as for the balanced density case in Section 5.2, except that we use the modified Gabor transform $\widetilde{T}$ of Proposition 5.7 with

$$ \displaystyle R_{y,\eta}=\frac{\langle y\rangle^{1/2}}{\langle\eta\rangle^{1/2}}. $$

We correspondingly use the vector-valued wave packets $\rho_{y,\eta},\tilde{\rho}_{y,\eta}$ and the function spaces $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}(\mathbf{R}^{d})$ from Section 5.3.

As in Section 5.2, we may assume $\sigma_{A},\sigma_{B}$ are orientation-preserving. Put

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{A}=\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\delta^{d}\det D\sigma_{A}(n)\Dirac_{\delta\sigma_{A}(n)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mu_{B}=\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\delta^{d}\det D\sigma_{B}(n)\Dirac_{\delta\sigma_{B}(n)}. $$

Let

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{y,\eta}=\begin{cases}\rho_{y,\eta}\mu_{A}&\mbox{if }\langle y\rangle^{p^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta\rangle^{q^{1/2}},\\
(\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}\mu_{B})^{\vee}&\mbox{if }\langle y\rangle^{p^{1/2}}<\langle\eta\rangle^{q^{1/2}}\end{cases} $$

(so $\nu_{y,\eta}$ is vector-valued). Then as usual, injectivity of $\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ follows from the following proposition.

#### Proposition 5.9.

Assume $s$ is sufficiently large, and $\delta$ is sufficiently small depending on $s$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta}\|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}. $$

#### Proof.

First consider the case $\langle y\rangle^{p^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta\rangle^{q^{1/2}}$ . Then $\nu_{y,\eta}=\rho_{y,\eta}\mu_{A}$ . We need pointwise bounds on

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|=|\langle\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta},\tilde{\rho}_{z,\zeta}\rangle|=\Big|\int\rho_{y,\eta}\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}_{z,\zeta}}\,\textnormal{d}\mu_{A}-\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\rho_{y,\eta}\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}_{z,\zeta}}\Big|. $$

The trivial bound is

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|\lesssim\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}+R_{z,\zeta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

We will apply this when $(z,\zeta)$ is in the complement of the region

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}=\{(z,\zeta)\in\mathbf{R}^{d}\times\mathbf{R}^{d}:|z-y|\lesssim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}\text{ and }|\zeta|\lesssim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{p+\varepsilon}\} $$

( $\varepsilon>0$ small and fixed).

Suppose now that $(z,\zeta)\in\mathcal{R}$ . Using the twisted Poisson summation formula (Lemma 5.4) to rewrite the right hand side of (5.22),

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|=\Big|\sum_{0\neq m\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\rho_{y,\eta}(x)\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}_{z,\zeta}(x)}e^{-2\pi im\cdot\sigma_{A}^{-1}(\delta^{-1}x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|. $$

Rescaling by $\delta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|=\delta^{d}\Big|\sum_{m\neq 0}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\rho_{y,\eta}(\delta x)\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}_{z,\zeta}(\delta x)}e^{-2\pi im\cdot\sigma_{A}^{-1}(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|. $$

Denote $\tau_{A}=\sigma_{A}^{-1}$ . Then $\tau_{A}$ is $(p+1)$ -pseudohomogeneous. Write

$$ \displaystyle\rho_{y,\eta}(x)=R_{y,\eta}^{-d/2}\rho\Big(\frac{x-y}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big)e^{2\pi i\eta\cdot x}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tilde{\rho}_{z,\zeta}(x)=R_{z,\zeta}^{-d/2}\tilde{\rho}\Big(\frac{x-z}{R_{z,\zeta}}\Big)e^{2\pi i\zeta\cdot x}, $$

with $\rho,\tilde{\rho}\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{R}^{d};\ell^{2})$ standard vector-valued Schwartz functions. Then

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|=\delta^{d}R_{y,\eta}^{-d/2}R_{z,\zeta}^{-d/2}\Big|\sum_{m\neq 0}\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\rho\Big(\frac{\delta x-y}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big)\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}\Big(\frac{\delta x-z}{R_{z,\zeta}}\Big)}e^{-2\pi i(\delta(\zeta-\eta)\cdot x+m\cdot\tau_{A}(x))}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|. $$

Let

$$ \displaystyle I=\Big|\int_{\mathbf{R}^{d}}\rho\Big(\frac{\delta x-y}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big)\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}\Big(\frac{\delta x-z}{R_{z,\zeta}}\Big)}e^{-2\pi i\phi(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big| $$

denote the absolute value of the integral, where

$$ \displaystyle\phi(x)=\delta(\zeta-\eta)\cdot x+m\cdot\tau_{A}(x) $$

is the phase. The gradient of the phase is

$$ \displaystyle\nabla\phi(x)=\delta(\zeta-\eta)+D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m. $$

We need bounds on $I$ for $(z,\zeta,m)\in\mathcal{R}\times(\mathbf{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\})$ . We split this into three regimes, each of which is treated differently:

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}\times(\mathbf{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\})=\mathcal{R}_{1}\cup\mathcal{R}_{2}\cup\mathcal{R}_{3}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{1} \displaystyle=\{(z,\zeta,m)\in\mathcal{R}\times(\mathbf{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\}):|m|\gtrsim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{p+2\varepsilon}\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{2} \displaystyle=\{(z,\zeta,m)\in\mathcal{R}\times(\mathbf{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\}):|m|\lesssim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{p+2\varepsilon}\text{ and }|\zeta|\not\sim\delta^{-p-1}|m|\langle y\rangle^{p}\}, \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{3} \displaystyle=\{(z,\zeta,m)\in\mathcal{R}\times(\mathbf{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\}):|m|\lesssim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{p+2\varepsilon}\text{ and }|\zeta|\sim\delta^{-p-1}|m|\langle y\rangle^{p}\}. $$

- 1. In $\mathcal{R}_{1}$ , we estimate $I$ by non-stationary phase everywhere.

- 2. In $\mathcal{R}_{2}$ , we estimate $I$ by non-stationary phase for $|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|$ , and by Schwartz decay elsewhere.

- 3. In $\mathcal{R}_{3}$ , we estimate $I$ by non-stationary phase when $x$ is closer to $\delta^{-1}z$ than the stationary point, and by Schwartz decay elsewhere.

The bulk of the mass of $\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})$ comes from $\mathcal{R}_{3}$ when the stationary point is close to $\delta^{-1}z$ , in which case the trivial bound for $I$ is sharp (up to inconsequential factors). Accordingly, the bounds for $I$ in the regime $\mathcal{R}_{3}$ are somewhat delicate, while in $\mathcal{R}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{R}_{2}$ they are straightforward.

First, suppose $(z,\zeta,m)\in\mathcal{R}_{1}$ . Then it follows from the $(p+1)$ -pseudohomogeneity of $\tau_{A}$ and the inequalities $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle^{p}$ and $|\zeta|\lesssim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{p+\varepsilon}$ that the term $D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m$ in (5.25) dominates, so

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)|\sim|D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m|\sim|m|\langle x\rangle^{p} $$

everywhere on $\mathbf{R}^{d}$ . Non-stationary phase (Corollary 5.2) then yields

$$ \displaystyle I\lesssim|m|^{-\infty}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

Second, suppose $(z,\zeta,m)\in\mathcal{R}_{2}$ . Then $1\leq|m|\lesssim\delta^{1-2\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{p+2\varepsilon}$ , so in particular $|y|\gtrsim\delta^{-\frac{1}{2p}}$ . Now that $y$ is somewhat large, the condition $(z,\zeta)\in\mathcal{R}$ implies $|z|\sim|y|$ . By Schwartz decay outside the region $\{x\in\mathbf{R}^{d}:|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|\}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle I\lesssim\Big|\int_{|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|}\rho\Big(\frac{\delta x-y}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big)\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}\Big(\frac{\delta x-z}{R_{z,\zeta}}\Big)}e^{-2\pi i\phi(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|+|y|^{-\infty}. $$

When $|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|$ , we have $|D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m|\sim\delta^{-p}|m||y|^{p}$ , so the condition $|\zeta|\not\sim\delta^{-p-1}|m|\langle y\rangle^{p}$ in the definition of $\mathcal{R}_{2}$ combined with $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle^{p}$ tells us that there is no cancellation in (5.25). Therefore

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)|\gtrsim|D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m|\sim|m|\langle x\rangle^{p} $$

for $|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|$ , and non-stationary phase (Corollary 5.2) again yields

$$ \displaystyle\Big|\int_{|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|}\rho\Big(\frac{\delta x-y}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big)\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}\Big(\frac{\delta x-z}{R_{z,\zeta}}\Big)}e^{-2\pi i\phi(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|\lesssim|m|^{-\infty}|y|^{-\infty} $$

(note that the region $\{|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|\}$ is much larger than the essential support of the integrand, so the implicit smooth cutoff to this region has harmless derivative growth). Hence

$$ \displaystyle I\lesssim|y|^{-\infty}\lesssim\delta^{\infty}|m|^{-\infty}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

Third, and finally, suppose $(z,\zeta,m)\in\mathcal{R}_{3}$ . Once again, $|y|\gtrsim\delta^{-\frac{1}{2p}}$ and $|z|\sim|y|$ . By the definition of $\mathcal{R}_{3}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\zeta|\sim\delta^{-p-1}|m|\langle y\rangle^{p}\geq\langle y\rangle^{p}\geq\langle\eta\rangle, $$

so

$$ \displaystyle R_{y,\eta}\gtrsim R_{z,\zeta}\sim\delta^{\frac{p+1}{2}}|m|^{-\frac{1}{2}}|y|^{\frac{1-p}{2}}. $$

Decompose $\mathbf{R}^{d}=\Omega_{\text{near}}\cup\Omega_{\text{far}}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\text{near}}=\{x\in\mathbf{R}^{d}:|x-\delta^{-1}z|\ll\delta^{p-1}|m|^{-1}|y|^{1-p}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|\} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\text{far}}=\{x\in\mathbf{R}^{d}:|x-\delta^{-1}z|\gtrsim\delta^{p-1}|m|^{-1}|y|^{1-p}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|\}. $$

Qualitatively, $\Omega_{\text{near}}$ consists of points $x\in\mathbf{R}^{d}$ which are near $\delta^{-1}z$ , while $\Omega_{\text{far}}$ consists of points which are far from $\delta^{-1}z$ . The precise threshold $\delta^{p-1}|m|^{-1}|y|^{1-p}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|$ will be motivated presently. Note first that by the $(p+1)$ -pseudohomogeneity of $\tau_{A}$ , the inequality $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle^{p}$ , and the fact that we are in $\mathcal{R}_{3}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|\lesssim\delta^{-p}|m||y|^{p}, $$

so

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\text{near}}\subseteq\{x\in\mathbf{R}^{d}:|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|\}. $$

Now for $|x|\sim\delta^{-1}|y|$ , we can use the fundamental theorem of calculus and pseudohomogeneity to estimate

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)-\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|=|D\tau_{A}(x)^{T}m-D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}z)^{T}m|\lesssim\delta^{1-p}|m||y|^{p-1}|x-\delta^{-1}z|. $$

Thus for $x\in\Omega_{\text{near}}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)-\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|\ll|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|, $$

and hence

$$ \displaystyle|\nabla\phi(x)|\sim|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|. $$

The estimate (5.29) is the motivation for the precise definition of $\Omega_{\text{near}}$ — we would like $\Omega_{\text{near}}$ to be as large as possible, but if we expanded it by even a large constant factor, then it could potentially contain a stationary point. Write $I\lesssim I_{\text{near}}+I_{\text{far}}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle I_{\text{near}}=\Big|\int_{\Omega_{\text{near}}}\rho\Big(\frac{\delta x-y}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big)\cdot\overline{\tilde{\rho}\Big(\frac{\delta x-z}{R_{z,\zeta}}\Big)}e^{-2\pi i\phi(x)}\,\textnormal{d}x\Big|, $$

and $I_{\text{far}}$ is defined similarly. Estimate $I_{\text{far}}$ trivially:

$$ \displaystyle I_{\text{far}}\lesssim\int_{\Omega_{\text{far}}}\Big\langle\frac{\delta x-y}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\Big\langle\frac{\delta x-z}{R_{z,\zeta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\,\textnormal{d}x \displaystyle\lesssim\delta^{-d}R_{z,\zeta}^{d}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\Big\langle\frac{\delta}{R_{z,\zeta}}\delta^{p-1}|m|^{-1}|y|^{1-p}\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)\Big\rangle^{-\infty} \displaystyle\sim\delta^{-d}R_{z,\zeta}^{d}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\langle\delta^{-1}R_{z,\zeta}\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)\rangle^{-\infty} $$

(here we’ve used (5.28) multiple times). Estimate $I_{\text{near}}$ by applying Proposition 5.3 with the parameters

$$ \displaystyle X \displaystyle=\delta^{-1}|y|, \displaystyle R \displaystyle=\min\{\delta^{-1}R_{z,\zeta},\delta^{p-1}|m|^{-1}|y|^{1-p}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|\}\lesssim X, \displaystyle V \displaystyle=\delta^{-d}R_{z,\zeta}^{d}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}, \displaystyle\lambda \displaystyle=|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|, \displaystyle M \displaystyle=|m|, \displaystyle r \displaystyle=p $$

(the second argument in the minimum in the definition of $R$ is necessary to capture the derivative bounds of the implicit smooth cutoff to $\Omega_{\text{near}}$ ). This yields the bound

$$ \displaystyle I_{\text{near}}\lesssim V\Big\langle\frac{\lambda R}{\langle\lambda^{-1}MRX^{r-1}\rangle}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

By (5.28) and our choice of parameters,

$$ \displaystyle\lambda R\sim\min\{\delta^{-1}R_{z,\zeta}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|,(\delta^{-1}R_{z,\zeta}|\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)|)^{2}\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lambda^{-1}MRX^{r-1}\lesssim 1, $$

so

$$ \displaystyle I_{\text{near}}\lesssim\delta^{-d}R_{z,\zeta}^{d}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\langle\delta^{-1}R_{z,\zeta}\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

Not coincidentally, this is the same bound we got for $I_{\text{far}}$ . Writing

$$ \displaystyle\delta^{-1}\nabla\phi(\delta^{-1}z)=\zeta-\eta+\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}z)^{T}m, $$

we conclude that

$$ \displaystyle I\lesssim I_{\text{near}}+I_{\text{far}}\lesssim\delta^{-d}R_{z,\zeta}^{d}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\langle R_{z,\zeta}(\zeta-\eta+\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}z)^{T}m)\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

Combining our estimates (5.26), (5.27), and (5.30) in the three regimes $\mathcal{R}_{1},\mathcal{R}_{2},\mathcal{R}_{3}$ , we obtain the bound

$$ \displaystyle I\lesssim|m|^{-\infty}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-\infty}+1_{\Big\{\begin{subarray}{c}|z|\sim|y|\gtrsim\delta^{-1/(2p)}\\
|\zeta|\sim\delta^{-p-1}|m|\langle y\rangle^{p}\end{subarray}\Big\}}\delta^{-d}R_{z,\zeta}^{d}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\langle R_{z,\zeta}(\zeta-\eta+\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}z)^{T}m)\rangle^{-\infty} $$

for all $(z,\zeta)\in\mathcal{R}$ and $m\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}\setminus\{0\}$ . Plugging this into (5.24),

$$ \displaystyle|\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)| \displaystyle\lesssim\delta^{(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2})d}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-\infty} \displaystyle\quad+\sum_{m\neq 0}1_{\Big\{\begin{subarray}{c}|z|\sim|y|\gtrsim\delta^{-1/(2p)}\\
|\zeta|\sim\delta^{-p-1}|m|\langle y\rangle^{p}\end{subarray}\Big\}}\Big(\frac{R_{z,\zeta}}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big)^{d/2}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\langle R_{z,\zeta}(\zeta-\eta+\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}z)^{T}m)\rangle^{-\infty}. $$

for $(z,\zeta)\in\mathcal{R}$ . Note that in the relevant regime $|z|\sim|y|\gtrsim\delta^{-\frac{1}{2p}}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle|\delta^{-1}D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}z)^{T}m-\eta|\sim\delta^{-1}|D\tau_{A}(\delta^{-1}z)^{T}m|\sim\delta^{-p-1}|m||y|^{p} $$

by pseudohomogeneity and the fact that $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle^{p}$ . Integrating (5.31) over $\mathcal{R}$ against the weight $\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}$ which appears in the definition of $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{R}}|\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta\lesssim_{s}\delta^{(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2})d}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}+\delta^{(p+1)(s-d/4)}\frac{\langle y\rangle^{pd/4}}{\langle\eta\rangle^{d/4}}\langle y\rangle^{-(p+1)s}. $$

On $\mathcal{R}^{c}$ , we use the trivial bound (5.23) to estimate

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{R}^{c}}|\widetilde{T}(\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta})(z,\zeta)|\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta \displaystyle\lesssim\int_{|z-y|\gtrsim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon}}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}+R_{z,\zeta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta \displaystyle\quad+\int_{|\zeta|\gtrsim\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{p+\varepsilon}}\Big\langle\frac{y-z}{R_{y,\eta}+R_{z,\zeta}}\Big\rangle^{-\infty}\langle z\rangle^{-s}\langle\zeta\rangle^{-s}\,\textnormal{d}z\,\textnormal{d}\zeta \displaystyle\lesssim_{s}\delta^{\infty}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}+R_{y,\eta}^{d}\langle y\rangle^{-s}(\delta^{-\varepsilon}\langle y\rangle^{p+\varepsilon})^{-(s-d)}. $$

Summing the two bounds above, and using as always that $R_{y,\eta}\leq\langle y\rangle^{1/2}$ and $\langle\eta\rangle\leq\langle y\rangle^{p}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta}\|_{\widetilde{S}^{-s}}\lesssim_{s}\Big[\delta^{(1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2})d}\langle y\rangle^{-\infty}+\delta^{(p+1)(s-d/4)}\frac{\langle y\rangle^{p(d/4-s)}}{\langle\eta\rangle^{d/4-s}}+\delta^{\varepsilon(s-d)}\langle y\rangle^{-\varepsilon(s-d)+(p+\frac{1}{2})d}\Big]\langle y\rangle^{-s}\langle\eta\rangle^{-s}. $$

Fixing $\varepsilon$ , taking $s$ large depending on $\varepsilon$ , and then taking $\delta$ small depending on $s$ , we finally obtain the desired bound (5.21).

It remains to treat the case where $\langle y\rangle^{p^{1/2}}<\langle\eta\rangle^{q^{1/2}}$ . We proceed similarly to the end of the proof of Proposition 4.4. In this case, $\nu_{y,\eta}=(\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}\mu_{B})^{\vee}$ , so by Proposition 5.8,

$$ \displaystyle\|\nu_{y,\eta}-\rho_{y,\eta}\|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}}=\|(\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}\mu_{B}-\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}})^{\vee}\|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}}\lesssim_{s}\|\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}\mu_{B}-\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}\|_{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}^{-s}}. $$

Denote $(y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})=(\eta,-y)$ . Then $\widehat{\rho_{y,\eta}}$ is an $L^{2}$ -normalized wave packet adapted to $B_{R_{y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}}(y^{\prime})\times B_{R_{y^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}^{-1}}(\eta^{\prime})$ in phase space. Now $\langle y^{\prime}\rangle^{q^{1/2}}\geq\langle\eta^{\prime}\rangle^{p^{1/2}}$ , so we can apply the above arguments with $p,q$ swapped to estimate the right hand side of (5.32). ∎

### 5.5. Completing the proof of Theorem 1.6

It remains to check that $\Coker\mathcal{F}_{A,B}$ is infinite-dimensional. Consider the subsets

$$ \displaystyle A^{\prime}=\{\delta\sigma_{A}(2n):n\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}\}\subseteq A\qquad\text{and}\qquad B^{\prime}=\{\delta\sigma_{B}(2n):n\in\mathbf{Z}^{d}\}\subseteq B. $$

Since $\delta$ is small, our work above shows that $\mathcal{F}_{A^{\prime},B^{\prime}}$ is injective. Now apply the same argument as in Section 4.4 to conclude.
